name: Diwali
timing: Around the new moon of the Hindu month of Kartika, usually October or November
summary: The festival of lights, marked by lamps, fireworks, family visits and large quantities of sweets.
story: Diwali is celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, and each tradition tells its own story of it. In many Hindu traditions it marks the return of Rama to Ayodhya, in others the worship of Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity. Houses are cleaned and lit with oil lamps, and families exchange gifts of sweets and dry fruit.
food_traditions: Homes prepare or buy sweets (mithai) and fried savoury snacks (farsan) in advance and share them with neighbours and relatives. Milk-based sweets such as gulab jamun, along with laddus and barfi, are common across regions, while the exact snacks vary by state.

name: Day of the Dead
timing: 1 to 2 November
duration: Two days, with preparations beginning earlier
summary: A Mexican celebration in which families remember the dead with altars (ofrendas), flowers and the foods their loved ones enjoyed.
story: The festivity blends pre-Hispanic indigenous beliefs about death with Catholic All Saints and All Souls observances. It is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. Families build altars at home and decorate graves, believing the dead return to visit.
food_traditions: Altars carry the favourite foods and drinks of the departed, plus pan de muerto, fruit, chocolate and sometimes mole. Foods are prepared in large amounts and shared among the living after the offering.

name: Carnevale
timing: The weeks before Lent, usually February or early March
duration: Varies by town, from days to weeks
summary: Italy's pre-Lent carnival, known for masks, parades and fried sweets. Venice and Viareggio are among the best-known celebrations.
story: Carnival comes from the period of feasting before the Lenten fast in the Christian calendar. Italian towns celebrate it with parades, costumes and masked balls, and each area has its own customs.
food_traditions: Fried sweets use up butter, eggs and sugar before Lent. They share the same idea under different names across Italy: chiacchiere, frappe, bugie, cenci, crostoli and others.

name: Ramadan in Morocco
timing: The ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, which moves about 11 days earlier each year
summary: The Muslim month of fasting from dawn to sunset. In Morocco the evening meal that breaks the fast has a well-known set of dishes, led by harira soup.
story: Ramadan is observed by Muslims worldwide as a month of fasting, prayer and charity. In Morocco, as elsewhere, families gather for the sunset meal (ftour) and a later meal before dawn. Because the Islamic calendar is lunar, Ramadan falls in a different season from year to year.
food_traditions: The fast is commonly broken with dates and milk or water, followed by harira, hard-boiled eggs, bread and sweet fried pastries such as chebakia. Sellou, a rich mix of toasted flour, almonds and sesame, is a popular energy-giving sweet during the month. Many households cook these in large quantities.

name: Mouloud (Mawlid) in Morocco
timing: 12th of Rabi al-awwal in the Islamic lunar calendar; moves about 11 days earlier each year
summary: The observance of the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad, celebrated in Morocco with family gatherings, religious chanting and festive food.
story: Mawlid is marked in many Muslim countries, though not by every community. In Morocco it is a public holiday and an occasion for family gatherings and religious processions. Local customs vary between towns and families.
food_traditions: Households often prepare a special meal, with couscous a common choice for a celebratory table, and sweets such as sellou are traditionally made and shared. Exact menus differ by family and region.

name: Fasika (Ethiopian Orthodox Easter)
timing: Orthodox Easter, set by the Ethiopian Orthodox church calendar; usually April or early May
duration: One day, following a long period of fasting
summary: The Ethiopian Orthodox celebration of Easter, ending a long Lenten fast of about 55 days with a festive meat meal.
story: Fasika is the most important feast of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo church. It follows a long fast, called Abiy Tsom, during which observant Christians eat no meat or dairy. The church services run late into Holy Saturday night, and in many households the fast is broken in the early hours of Easter Sunday.
food_traditions: The fast-breaking meal centres on doro wat, a chicken stew with boiled eggs, served with injera and often with home-brewed tej or other drinks. Many families also slaughter a sheep or ox and share the meat with neighbours and relatives. During the preceding fast, vegan dishes such as shiro, misir wat and gomen make up daily meals, which is why they are linked here as seasonal foods.

name: Meskel
timing: 17 Meskerem in the Ethiopian calendar, which is 27 September (28 September in some years)
duration: One day, with a bonfire on the eve
summary: A religious festival recalling the finding of the True Cross, marked by a large bonfire, processions and a family feast.
story: Meskel commemorates the finding of the cross on which Jesus was crucified, according to Christian tradition. It is celebrated by the Ethiopian Orthodox church and also in Eritrea. On the eve, communities build a tall pile of branches called demera, decorated with flowers, which is lit after prayers and songs. UNESCO recognises Meskel as intangible cultural heritage.
food_traditions: Families gather for a festive meal after the bonfire. Meat dishes such as kitfo and tibs are typical of Ethiopian feasts and are commonly served at holiday gatherings, with injera and home-brewed drinks. Menus differ by household and region.

name: Sham el-Nessim
timing: The Monday after Coptic Orthodox Easter, usually April or May
summary: A spring holiday celebrated by Egyptians of all faiths with picnics outdoors, coloured eggs and salted and fermented fish.
story: Sham el-Nessim is a national spring holiday on the Monday after Coptic Easter. Its name is commonly interpreted as meaning something like 'smelling the breeze'. Egyptians often link it to ancient spring festivals, a connection that is widely repeated but difficult to prove in detail. Families go to parks, the Nile and the countryside.
food_traditions: Traditional foods include fesikh (fermented salted mullet) and other salted fish such as renga, boiled and coloured eggs, spring onions and lettuce. The meal is eaten outdoors. Fesikh is a seasonal speciality that must be bought from a reputable producer, since incorrectly prepared salted fish can cause serious food poisoning.

name: Eid celebrations in Egypt
timing: Eid al-Fitr (1 Shawwal, ending Ramadan) and Eid al-Adha (10 Dhu al-Hijjah) in the Islamic lunar calendar; both move about 11 days earlier each year
summary: The two main Islamic holidays, celebrated in Egypt with family visits and foods that include sweet biscuits for Eid al-Fitr and meat dishes for Eid al-Adha.
story: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha follows the pilgrimage season and commemorates the story of Ibrahim and his son. Both are public holidays in Egypt. Families gather, give gifts and visit relatives.
food_traditions: Making kahk, buttery biscuits often filled with dates or nuts and dusted with sugar, is a long-standing practice in the days before Eid al-Fitr. At Eid al-Adha, families who sacrifice an animal share the meat, and fattah of rice, bread and meat is a well-known dish for the occasion.

name: New Yam Festival (Iri Ji)
timing: Late in the rainy season at the yam harvest, roughly August to October; the date is set locally by each community
duration: Usually a day to several days, depending on the community
summary: A harvest thanksgiving in which Igbo communities give thanks for the first yams of the season before they are eaten. Similar new yam festivals are held by other groups in West Africa under different names.
story: Among the Igbo, yam has long been treated as a prestige crop, and the first harvest is marked with rituals before anyone eats freely from it. Traditionally the festival is presided over by an elder or chief, who gives thanks and offers the first yam, and in many communities it also includes masquerades, dancing and gatherings of extended families. Today it is observed by Christian and traditional communities alike, and details differ from town to town.
food_traditions: The new yam is roasted or boiled and eaten with palm oil and pepper sauce, often followed by yam with soups and stews. Food is shared widely with visitors and kin, and the first serving often has a ritual role before the general meal.

name: Eid al-Adha in northern Nigeria
timing: 10 Dhu al-Hijjah in the Islamic lunar calendar, so it moves about 11 days earlier each year
duration: Two to three days of celebration
summary: Muslim families mark the festival of sacrifice with prayers, the slaughter of a ram or other animal, and shared meat. In the Hausa-speaking north it is called Babbar Sallah, the big prayer, and some emirates hold horse-riding durbar displays around the Eid holidays.
story: Eid al-Adha commemorates the willingness of Ibrahim to sacrifice his son, and it falls at the end of the Hajj season. In northern Nigeria the day begins with congregational prayer, and the sacrificed animal is divided between the household, relatives and the poor. Durbar, a parade of mounted riders in ceremonial dress at the emirs' palaces, is traditionally tied to the Eid festivals in cities such as Kano and Katsina.
food_traditions: Meat from the sacrificed animal is cooked in many forms across a few days: grilled, stewed, or as suya-style roasts, and served with rice dishes. Fura da nono and other milk drinks are common refreshments in many Hausa and Fulani households. Exact menus vary by family.

name: Heritage Day / National Braai Day
timing: 24 September each year
summary: A South African public holiday celebrating the country's diverse cultures, which in practice is marked by families and friends gathering for a braai (barbecue).
story: Heritage Day is a public holiday meant to celebrate the cultural diversity of the nation's many communities. The braai, an outdoor fire-cooked meal found in nearly every South African culture, became widely linked with the day, and in the 2000s a campaign encouraged people to treat 24 September as National Braai Day as a unifying tradition. Not everyone agrees on this emphasis, and many people mark the day with traditional dress, music and community events instead.
food_traditions: Meat is grilled over wood or charcoal, most often boerewors, chops and steak, and served with pap or bread and relishes such as chakalaka. Many families also cook potjiekos or bring dishes from their own heritage to share.

name: Eid al-Fitr in the Cape Malay community
timing: 1 Shawwal in the Islamic lunar calendar, the day after Ramadan ends; it moves about 11 days earlier each year
summary: The festival that ends the Ramadan fast is marked in Cape Town's Cape Malay community with prayers, family visits and tables of homemade sweets and savouries.
story: Muslims have lived at the Cape since the Dutch colonial period, when many were brought as enslaved people, political exiles and skilled workers from South and Southeast Asia and Africa. Their descendants, known as Cape Malays, preserve distinct religious and culinary traditions. After the month-long fast, families gather for morning prayer, visit relatives, and offer visitors food.
food_traditions: Koesisters, sweet spiced dough dipped in syrup and rolled in coconut, are a classic holiday treat, alongside samoosas, biscuits and rich family meals. The exact table varies by household.

name: Eid al-Fitr
timing: First day of Shawwal in the Islamic lunar calendar, so it moves about 11 days earlier each year
summary: The Muslim festival that ends the month of Ramadan fasting, marked by prayers, family visits and feasts.
story: Eid al-Fitr is celebrated by Muslims around the world after Ramadan. In India, which has one of the largest Muslim populations in the world, it is a public holiday and a major family occasion, observed with congregational prayers, new clothes and charity.
food_traditions: Sweets such as sheer khurma (a vermicelli and milk dessert) are widely prepared, and many households serve festive meat dishes for guests. In Hyderabad, biryani and in Kashmir, slow-cooked meat dishes such as rogan josh are common celebratory dishes, though what is cooked varies by family and community.

name: Chinese New Year
timing: Begins on the new moon of the first lunar month, between late January and mid-February
duration: Traditionally about 15 days, ending with the Lantern Festival
summary: The most important traditional holiday in China, centred on the family reunion dinner and food with symbolic meanings.
story: Chinese New Year, known in China as the Spring Festival, marks the start of the lunar new year. Millions travel home to be with family. Customs include cleaning the house beforehand, giving red envelopes, lighting firecrackers and visiting relatives. UNESCO has inscribed Spring Festival practices on its intangible heritage list.
food_traditions: The reunion dinner on New Year's Eve is the key meal. In the north, families make and eat jiaozi dumplings, often together; in many regions, nian gao is eaten because its name sounds like a phrase meaning higher year by year. Foods are chosen for wordplay and symbolism, and customs vary widely by region and family.

name: Oshogatsu (Japanese New Year)
timing: 1 January, with celebrations from 31 December through about 3 January
duration: Several days, traditionally 1 to 3 January as the main days
summary: Japan's New Year, the most important annual holiday, observed with temple visits, family gatherings and special foods.
story: Oshogatsu is a time for families to gather, visit shrines or temples for the first visit of the year (hatsumode), and begin the year afresh. Houses are cleaned before the new year. Many businesses close for several days, which is part of why traditional foods are prepared that keep well. UNESCO recognises washoku and its link with New Year celebrations.
food_traditions: Osechi ryori is a set of small dishes packed in tiered boxes, each linked to wishes such as health or good fortune. Black soybeans (kuromame) stand for diligence and health. Ozoni, a soup with rice cake, is eaten on New Year morning in a form that differs by region. On New Year's Eve, many people eat toshikoshi soba.

name: Songkran
timing: 13 to 15 April, the traditional Thai new year
duration: Three days, sometimes longer in places
summary: The Thai new year, marked by water throwing, temple visits and family gatherings during the hottest season.
story: Songkran is rooted in the traditional solar new year observed in several Southeast Asian countries. In Thailand it is a time to return to family homes, clean houses, make merit at Buddhist temples and pour scented water over Buddha images and over the hands of elders as a sign of respect. The playful public water fights are a more recent and popular extension of those blessings, linked to the heat of April.
food_traditions: Families prepare food to offer to monks and to share. In some communities, notably Mon ones, khao chae with its chilled scented water and side dishes is made. Seasonal sweets and fruit, including ripe mango, are common at this time of year.

name: Tết
timing: Lunar new year, between late January and mid February
duration: Several days, with preparations for weeks beforehand
summary: The Vietnamese Lunar New Year, the most important family holiday of the year.
story: Tết marks the first day of the lunar new year. Families clean their homes, settle debts, visit ancestral altars and travel to be with relatives. It is celebrated with flowers such as peach blossom in the north and apricot blossom in the south, and with gifts of lucky money.
food_traditions: Special foods include bánh chưng in the north and the similar cylindrical bánh tét in the south, braised pork, pickled vegetables and sweet candied fruits. Making and tending to the pot of bánh chưng is itself a family tradition.

name: Natale (Christmas in Italy)
timing: Advent through Epiphany, with the main meals on 24 and 25 December
summary: Italy's Christmas season, marked by family meals and sweet breads like panettone and pandoro.
story: Christmas is a major religious and family holiday in Italy. Customs differ by region, from the Christmas Eve fish meal in much of the south to elaborate stuffed pasta and broths in the north. Nativity scenes and Christmas markets are common.
food_traditions: Panettone from Milan and pandoro from Verona are given as gifts and served after the festive meal across Italy, often with sweet sparkling wine or mascarpone cream.

name: Chandeleur
timing: 2 February
summary: The French feast of Candlemas, celebrated by making and eating crêpes.
story: Chandeleur is the Christian feast of Candlemas, held 40 days after Christmas. In France it has long been tied to the custom of making crêpes at home, and to sayings about weather and the coming spring.
food_traditions: Families make stacks of crêpes. A custom holds that flipping the first crêpe with a coin in the other hand brings prosperity for the year. In Brittany, savoury buckwheat galettes are also common.

name: Épiphanie (Epiphany)
timing: 6 January, or the first Sunday of January; eaten through the month
summary: The Christian feast of the three kings, marked in France by sharing a galette des rois with a hidden charm.
story: Epiphany commemorates the visit of the Magi in the Christian tradition. In France it is celebrated with a cake, and the person who finds the hidden fève becomes king or queen for the day.
food_traditions: Pastry shops sell galettes des rois throughout January; families and workplaces buy one to share. In the south, a ring-shaped brioche is more usual.

name: Oktoberfest
timing: Late September to the first weekend of October, in Munich
summary: Munich's huge annual beer festival, with beer tents, a funfair and a menu of traditional Bavarian food.
story: Oktoberfest began in 1810 with the royal wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria and Princess Therese, celebrated with horse races in a meadow outside Munich (the Theresienwiese, or Wiesn). It became an annual fair and over time grew into the world's largest beer festival, with large tents run by Munich breweries.
food_traditions: Tent menus centre on Bavarian staples: roast chicken (Hendl), pork roasts, pretzels, cheese dishes and sweets. Beer is served in litre mugs from Munich breweries. Weisswurst, a morning sausage, is eaten in the early hours.

name: Christmas markets
timing: From late November to Christmas Eve
summary: Germany's Advent markets, with stalls selling gingerbread, stollen, roasted nuts and mulled wine.
story: Christmas markets have a long history in German-speaking lands, with the Dresden Striezelmarkt and Nuremberg Christkindlesmarkt among the best known. They fill town squares during Advent with stalls, lights and crafts.
food_traditions: Stalls sell regional Christmas baking such as stollen and lebkuchen, as well as roasted almonds, sausages and mulled wine (Glühwein). Each city has its own specialities.

name: Semana Santa (Holy Week)
timing: The week before Easter Sunday, March or April
summary: The Holy Week before Easter, marked in Spanish towns by solemn processions of religious images, with especially large celebrations in Andalusia.
story: Semana Santa commemorates the last days of Christ in the Christian calendar. In Spanish towns, brotherhoods called cofradías carry sculpted floats through the streets in processions, often accompanied by music. Seville, Málaga and many other cities are known for their celebrations, though customs vary from place to place.
food_traditions: Lent and Holy Week traditionally avoided meat, so sweets and fish dishes mark the season. Torrijas are baked or fried in homes and pastry shops, and in Andalusia pestiños are a classic sweet of the season.

name: Las Fallas
timing: Mid-March, climaxing on 19 March
duration: About a week, with the main days from 15 to 19 March
summary: Valencia's spring festival of giant satirical papier-mâché sculptures, fireworks and music, which end with the sculptures being burned on the night of 19 March.
story: The Fallas are linked to the feast of Saint Joseph on 19 March. Neighbourhood groups, called falles, build large sculptures that are paraded and finally burned. The origins are often traced to older spring bonfires and carpenters' traditions; the exact beginnings are uncertain. UNESCO inscribed the festivity on its intangible heritage list in 2016.
food_traditions: Street stalls fry buñuelos de calabaza for crowds, usually with thick hot chocolate, while neighbourhood groups cook communal paellas.

name: Greek Orthodox Easter
timing: Sunday after Passover in the Orthodox calendar, between early April and early May
duration: Holy Week, with the main celebrations from Holy Thursday to Easter Sunday
summary: The most important festival of the Greek year, celebrating the Resurrection after the long Lenten fast, with midnight services, red eggs, and a lamb feast.
story: Orthodox Easter (Pascha) is calculated using a different calendar from most Western churches, so it often falls on a different date. Holy Week includes services each day, and the Resurrection service on Saturday night ends with candlelight and the greeting Christos Anesti. Families then break the fast.
food_traditions: Red-dyed eggs are cracked against each other, tsoureki is baked, magiritsa is eaten after midnight service, and lamb or goat is roasted on Easter Sunday.

name: Clean Monday
timing: Seven weeks before Orthodox Easter, between February and March
summary: The first day of Orthodox Lent and a public holiday in Greece, marked by outdoor picnics, kite-flying and meat-free food.
story: Clean Monday begins the Great Lent. People traditionally go to the countryside for picnics and fly kites. The day follows the carnival period, Apokries, and meat and dairy are set aside.
food_traditions: The meal is fasting food: taramosalata, olives, pickles, beans, shellfish and octopus, and lagana, a flat unleavened bread baked only on this day.

name: Mexican Independence Day
timing: 15 to 16 September
summary: Mexico's national holiday marking the start of the war of independence from Spain in 1810, celebrated with fireworks, flags and big family meals.
story: On the night of 15 September, Mexicans gather in town squares to hear the Grito de Dolores, a re-enactment of the call to arms attributed to the priest Miguel Hidalgo in 1810, and the celebrations continue through 16 September. Streets and homes are decorated in green, white and red. The date marks the beginning of a war that ended with independence in 1821, rather than independence itself.
food_traditions: Families and restaurants prepare dishes whose colours echo the flag. Pozole is a standard dish of the celebration, served in large bowls with garnishes, and chiles en nogada, in season in late summer, is its showpiece in Puebla and beyond. Street vendors sell antojitos, and tequila and mezcal are poured.

name: Thanksgiving
timing: Fourth Thursday of November
duration: One day, often a long weekend
summary: A national holiday of family gatherings and a large shared meal, with roots in harvest celebrations and a day of thanks.
story: Thanksgiving is observed on the fourth Thursday of November. It is traditionally linked to a harvest feast held at Plymouth in 1621 between English settlers and the Wampanoag people, though thanksgiving observances in various forms were held across the colonies, and the holiday as we know it was shaped in the 19th century and declared a national holiday in 1863. For many Native Americans the holiday is also a time to remember the history of colonisation, and some observe a day of mourning. Today it centres on family and travel.
food_traditions: The meal centres on roast turkey, with stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy, cranberry sauce, vegetables and breads, and a table of pies, pumpkin pie most of all. Regional and family dishes, such as cornbread dressing in the South or sweet potato casserole, vary widely.

name: Mardi Gras
timing: The day before Ash Wednesday, usually February or March, with the Carnival season beginning on 6 January
duration: A season of weeks, peaking in the days before Mardi Gras
summary: The climax of Carnival season in Louisiana, with parades, costumes, music and shared meals.
story: Mardi Gras (Fat Tuesday) is the last day before the Christian season of Lent, and in New Orleans and other Louisiana communities it ends a Carnival season of parades, balls and street celebrations. The traditions come from French Catholic roots in Louisiana and have been shaped by local krewes, Black Mardi Gras Indians, and the Cajun country Courir de Mardi Gras. Different communities mark the day in different ways.
food_traditions: Feasting before Lent is the heart of the day. King cake, a ring-shaped pastry, is the best-known seasonal sweet. Gumbo and jambalaya are made in large pots for crowds, for parade-watching and for gatherings of family and friends.

name: Sugar shack season
timing: Late winter to early spring, usually March and April, when maple sap runs
duration: Several weeks, depending on the weather
summary: The spring maple harvest in Quebec, celebrated with traditional meals in sugar shacks (cabanes à sucre).
story: Maple sap runs when nights are below freezing and days are warm, and Quebec produces a large share of the world's maple syrup. The harvest was learned from Indigenous peoples of the north-east, and it later became a tradition of the French-Canadian countryside to gather at a sugar shack to eat and celebrate the end of winter. Many sugar shacks are now open to the public with set menus, music and demonstrations.
food_traditions: Menus are hearty and centre on maple: baked beans, ham, eggs, pancakes, pickles and soup, with maple syrup poured over almost anything. Dessert includes pouding chômeur and maple taffy poured on snow, wound on a stick.

name: Christmas Eve réveillon
timing: 24 December, after midnight mass in tradition; also New Year's Eve
summary: A long family supper held after midnight mass on Christmas Eve, a deeply rooted French-Canadian tradition.
story: The réveillon (from the French for waking) is a late meal after the midnight mass on Christmas Eve. In Quebec it has been a family feast for generations, and it is repeated on New Year's Eve. Many families keep it up even as church attendance has declined, and recipes are handed down in the family.
food_traditions: Tourtière is the signature dish, often served with ketchup or chutney. Other dishes vary by family and region, and may include ragoût de pattes de cochon (pork hock stew), baked ham, pickles and a log-shaped Christmas cake called the bûche de Noël.

name: Nochebuena
timing: 24 December, the evening of Christmas Eve
summary: The Christmas Eve family dinner, which is the main food celebration of the Cuban Christmas season.
story: Nochebuena, meaning the good night, is the Christmas Eve meal observed across the Spanish-speaking world. In Cuba it is the largest family gathering of the year. Public celebration of Christmas was limited for several decades in the later 20th century, and the holiday has been restored as a public holiday since the late 1990s, though home Nochebuena dinners continued throughout.
food_traditions: Roast pork is the traditional centrepiece, often a whole pig or a shoulder marinated in garlic and sour orange. Typical sides are rice cooked with beans, boiled cassava with mojo, and fried plantain. Flan and other sweets close the meal.

name: Christmas in Jamaica
timing: 25 December, with celebrations through December
summary: A season of family meals, church services, street markets and special drinks and baking.
story: Christmas in Jamaica combines Christian observance with long-standing island traditions, such as Grand Market on Christmas Eve, new clothes, and the baking of rich fruit cake soaked in rum and wine. Families travel home, houses are cleaned and repainted, and the food reflects the island's mixed heritage.
food_traditions: Christmas dinner often includes rice and peas, baked ham or chicken, and curried goat, with sorrel drink and the dark Christmas cake. Sorrel is made in advance, steeped overnight and served chilled.

name: Easter in Jamaica
timing: Good Friday to Easter Monday, March or April
summary: The Easter weekend, when Jamaicans traditionally eat fish on Good Friday and spiced bun and cheese through the holiday.
story: Easter is observed by Christians across Jamaica, with church services, family outings and beach trips. It is a public holiday weekend, and bakeries and shops sell large quantities of spiced buns.
food_traditions: Fish, especially fried or escovitch fish, is eaten on Good Friday in place of meat. Spiced bun with a slice of processed cheese is the most distinctive Easter food and is eaten throughout the holiday weekend.

name: Australia Day
timing: 26 January
summary: The national day, marked in the summer heat with barbecues, beach trips, and community events.
story: 26 January marks the arrival of the First Fleet at Sydney Cove in 1788. For many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people it is a day of mourning or protest and is also called Invasion Day or Survival Day, and there is ongoing public debate about the date. Many Australians mark it as a public holiday with family gatherings.
food_traditions: The usual meal is an outdoor barbecue with sausages, steak, and salads, followed by lamingtons. Sausage sizzles are also run by local groups to raise funds.

name: Anzac Day
timing: 25 April
summary: A day of remembrance for Australians and New Zealanders who served and died in war, held each year on 25 April.
story: The date marks the 1915 landings at Gallipoli during the First World War and has grown into a day to remember all who served. Dawn services and marches are held across the country. It is a solemn occasion.
food_traditions: Food is secondary to the commemoration, but Anzac biscuits are widely baked and eaten around the day, and some communities hold a gunfire breakfast after the dawn service.

name: Matariki
timing: Midwinter, when the Matariki star cluster (Pleiades) rises; a public holiday on a Friday in late June or July, set each year
duration: Several days of events; one public holiday
summary: The Māori New Year, marked by the rising of the Matariki star cluster in midwinter.
story: Matariki is the Māori name for the Pleiades star cluster, whose pre-dawn rising in midwinter has long marked the turn of the year in Māori tradition. It is a time to remember those who have died, celebrate the present and look to the year ahead. Matariki became a New Zealand public holiday in 2022, and its date changes each year following the lunar calendar.
food_traditions: Gathering and sharing food is central. Traditionally the harvest of crops such as kūmara was linked to Matariki's stars, and a hāngī is a common feast at community events. The steam from the hāngī is sometimes said to nourish the stars. Different iwi (tribes) have their own customs.

name: Waitangi Day
timing: 6 February
summary: New Zealand's national day, commemorating the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840.
story: On 6 February 1840 representatives of the British Crown and many Māori chiefs began signing the Treaty of Waitangi at Waitangi in the Bay of Islands. Its meaning and the way it has been honoured are still discussed today. The day is marked with ceremonies at Waitangi and events around the country, and views of it differ.
food_traditions: Community events and gatherings often serve a hāngī and fried bread, along with barbecues and other shared meals.

name: Diwali in Fiji
timing: Around the new moon of the Hindu month of Kartika, in October or November; a public holiday
duration: One public holiday, with celebrations over several days
summary: The festival of lights, widely celebrated by Fiji's Indo-Fijian community and a national public holiday.
story: Diwali is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, and arrived in Fiji with Indian indentured labourers from 1879. Homes and shops are cleaned, decorated with lamps and lights, and families visit one another. It is a public holiday in Fiji, and people of other backgrounds often join the festivities.
food_traditions: Families make and exchange sweets such as ladoo and fried snacks such as samosas, and share vegetarian meals. Sweets are given to neighbours and friends as gifts.

name: Fiji Day
timing: 10 October
duration: One day, with celebrations in the preceding week
summary: Fiji's national day, marking independence from Britain in 1970.
story: Fiji became independent from Britain on 10 October 1970. The day is marked with ceremonies, parades, performances, and family gatherings across the islands.
food_traditions: Celebrations often include a lovo or shared feasts, kava drinking, and raw-fish kokoda. Menus vary by community and household.

name: White Sunday
timing: A Sunday in October, usually the second Sunday of the month
summary: A Samoan holiday dedicated to children, who wear white, lead the church service and are served the best food.
story: White Sunday (Lotu a Tamaiti, the children's church service) is a Christian celebration of children observed across Samoa and by Samoan communities abroad. Children dress in white, recite and perform in church and are the focus of the day. It reflects the central role of the church in Samoan life.
food_traditions: After church a large family meal is prepared, usually from the umu. Children are traditionally served first and given the best of the food, with adults eating afterwards. Typical dishes are roast pork, palusami, fish dishes, breadfruit and taro, along with sweet items such as coconut buns.

name: Samoa Independence Celebrations
timing: Early June, marking independence in 1962
summary: National celebrations in early June, with cultural events, competitions and feasting across Samoa.
story: Samoa became independent in 1962, the first Pacific island nation to do so after a period of colonial administration. The anniversary is celebrated in early June with several days of public events, including cultural performances and sporting competitions.
food_traditions: Food is shared at official events, village gatherings and family meals, with umu dishes and fresh seafood prominent. As elsewhere in Samoa, hosting generously is part of fa'a Samoa.

name: Heilala Festival
timing: July, in the week around the King's birthday
summary: Tonga's main annual festival, held in July with parades, music, sport and community feasts.
story: The Heilala Festival is a week-long celebration in Tonga, centred on the capital Nuku'alofa and held in July around the King's birthday. It is named after the heilala, a flower used in garlands and perfume that is a national symbol. Events include parades, performances and competitions.
food_traditions: Celebrations are accompanied by feasts at which roast pork, lu, root crops, raw fish and cold drinks are shared. Feast food at such occasions follows the same pattern as other Tongan celebrations.

name: Festa Junina
timing: Throughout June, around the feast days of St Anthony (13 June), St John (24 June) and St Peter (29 June)
summary: Brazil's June festivals, with bonfires, square dancing, costumes and large amounts of corn-based food.
story: Festa Junina (also called Festa de Sao Joao) was brought by the Portuguese and is linked to the Catholic feasts of Saints Anthony, John and Peter, which in turn overlap with older European midsummer celebrations. In Brazil it became a rural-themed party with dances such as the quadrilha, and it is especially large in the North-East, in cities such as Caruaru and Campina Grande. Schools, parishes and neighbourhoods hold their own arraiais (festival grounds).
food_traditions: June coincides with the corn harvest in much of the country, so the food is mostly corn: canjica and pamonha, corn cake, popcorn and roasted corn on the cob. Sweets such as pe-de-moleque (peanut brittle) and drinks like quentao (spiced hot cane spirit) are also typical.

name: Lord of Miracles
timing: Processions through Lima during October, with the main days around mid-October, sometimes continuing into early November
summary: Lima's great purple-clad Catholic procession in honour of the Lord of Miracles, with a strong food tradition.
story: The festival centres on an image of Christ painted on a wall in the colonial period, traditionally attributed to an enslaved man of Angolan origin. According to tradition the wall survived a major 17th-century earthquake in Lima, and a cult grew around it. Each October large processions carry a replica through the streets, with devotees in purple. It is one of the largest religious events in Peru.
food_traditions: Stalls along the route sell anticuchos, picarones (fried squash and sweet potato rings), and the festival's signature sweet, turron de Dona Pepa. Many families prepare these at home during the month.

name: Fiesta de San Juan
timing: 24 June
duration: One day, often with several days of celebration
summary: The feast of St John the Baptist, the main festival of the Peruvian jungle, celebrated with river bathing, music and juane.
story: In Amazonian towns such as Pucallpa, Iquitos and Tarapoto, 24 June is the feast of San Juan, celebrated with community gatherings, music and ritual bathing in rivers in honour of the saint. It has also become a day of regional pride and a celebration of local jungle food.
food_traditions: Juane, the leaf-wrapped rice and chicken parcel, is the festival's iconic food and is eaten widely on San Juan, to the point that the day's menu is sometimes called by its name.

name: 25 de Mayo
local_name: Día de la Revolución de Mayo
timing: 25 May, a national holiday
summary: Argentina's national holiday marking the start of the move to independence, celebrated with patriotic acts and traditional food.
story: The holiday commemorates the 1810 May Revolution in Buenos Aires, when the colonial viceroy was replaced by a local governing council, an early step in the process that led to independence in 1816. It falls in the cool autumn, and families gather for lunch and watch public events.
food_traditions: Locro is the classic dish of the day, especially in the North-West, and empanadas are common. In the afternoon, pastelitos criollos are eaten with mate or hot chocolate.

name: Day of the Pachamama
timing: 1 August, throughout the month in Andean communities
duration: One day, with rites through August
summary: The Andean ritual honouring Pachamama, Mother Earth, held in the North-West at the start of the sowing season.
story: Pachamama is an earth deity in the Andean tradition. In Jujuy, Salta and nearby areas, communities make offerings in August, burying food, drink and coca leaves in a hole in the ground in thanks and to ask for fertility of the land and animals. Today it is often blended with Catholic practice.
food_traditions: Communal meals are shared after the offering. Corn-based dishes such as locro and humita are typical of northern festive tables, although menus vary by community and household.

name: Carnaval de Barranquilla
timing: The four days before Ash Wednesday, in February or March
duration: Four days, with weeks of preparatory events
summary: One of the largest carnivals in Latin America, with parades, music, dance and masks on the Caribbean coast.
story: Carnaval de Barranquilla grew out of colonial-era celebrations on the Caribbean coast and combines Spanish, African and indigenous traditions. It features parades such as the Batalla de Flores and dances like the cumbia. UNESCO recognised the carnival as a masterpiece of intangible heritage in the early 2000s, and it is now on the Representative List.
food_traditions: Street vendors and family kitchens sell fried snacks and regional food through the festivities, including arepas de huevo and patacones, along with cold drinks and fruit. Food is part of the festival atmosphere but is not tied to one fixed menu.

name: Christmas novena (Novena de Aguinaldos)
timing: 16 to 24 December
summary: Nine evenings of prayer and carols before Christmas, held in homes and neighbourhoods with shared food.
story: The novena is a Catholic devotion of nine days of prayers and songs (villancicos) leading to Christmas. In Colombia families, neighbours and friends gather each evening, and the tradition has become a major social occasion. Details of the customs differ from region to region.
food_traditions: Buñuelos and natilla are the classic sweet pairing of the novena and the Christmas season. Other seasonal foods such as hot chocolate and, in some regions, tamales or roast pork are also served.

name: Fiestas Patrias
timing: 18 and 19 September, often extended into a long weekend or week
duration: Two main days, often a week of celebrations
summary: Chile's national independence celebrations, marked with fondas, folk dancing (cueca) and large family barbecues.
story: The Fiestas Patrias commemorate the first national government junta of 18 September 1810, the first step toward independence from Spain, and the Armed Forces on 19 September. Public spaces are filled with temporary taverns called fondas and ramadas, with music, dancing the cueca, and the flying of kites.
food_traditions: Fondas serve empanadas de pino, grilled meats and chicha, along with refreshing drinks such as mote con huesillo. Families cook asados at home. Menus vary by region and family.

name: Chiloé costumbrista festivals
timing: Mainly in the southern summer, January to March
duration: Single days or weekends, held in different villages
summary: Community festivals across Chiloé that celebrate island traditions, crafts and food, with curanto as the central dish.
story: These local festivals, usually held in summer in different villages of the island, showcase rural traditions of the archipelago including music, crafts, boat and farming skills and cooking. They are organised by local communities. The dates and names vary by place.
food_traditions: Curanto, often cooked in a pit, is the main attraction, along with potato breads such as milcao and chapaleles, smoked meats and seafood.
